name: Abhishek Gupta

papers.title: Q-OIL: Optimistic Exploration in Learning from Human Interventions
papers.abstract: As robots are deployed in the real world, they will inevitably make mistakes. Human interventions provide valuable feedback for improving their behavior, enabling them to adapt online to new scenarios. However, studying human-in-the-loop robot learning is difficult: real-world experiments are slow and expensive, so most algorithm development relies on simulated human models. We show that common human modeling assumptions do not match how real people intervene in practice. Through an analysis of intervention data from human participants, we find that humans tend to intervene when agent progress stalls, and that their corrective actions are often suboptimal. Motivated by these findings, we introduce a progress-based model of human intervention that achieves higher rank correlation with real-user algorithm rankings, enabling realistic algorithm benchmarking and development in simulation. Driven by these insights, we identify shortcomings in prior methods for learning from interventions and propose Q-OIL, a method that introduces optimistic bonuses on intervention transitions in reinforcement learning, encouraging the agent to revisit and learn from informative intervention states. We show that with the right design choices, including decoupled critics to avoid over-optimism and imitation-learning regularization, our proposed method learns more efficiently than competitive baselines, achieving 10-50% higher success in simulation and on real-world robotic tasks. By grounding both evaluation and learning in realistic human behavior, this work provides a practical path toward scalable robot learning from interventions.

papers.title: A Balanced Data Diet: Addressing the Bottleneck in Mega-Scale RL for Robot Control
papers.abstract: General-purpose robots must perform a wide range of tasks from agile locomotion to dexterous manipulation, but current sim2real RL pipelines depend on per-task structural priors to train such as shaped rewards and demonstrations. Recent work has shown that diverse simulator resets, combined with massively parallel simulation, can replace much of this engineering. Yet, uniformly sampling over this distribution wastes a growing fraction of environments on task configurations the policy has already mastered or cannot yet attempt, so returns flatten when scaling the number of parallel environments. We introduce a simple adaptive sampler, Success Guided Sampling (SGS), that tracks the policy's frontier of capability, concentrating experience on task configurations where success rate sits in a productive band. This results in continued performance gains up to 1M+ parallel environments, 16× beyond prior work, under simple reward structures and no demonstrations. We demonstrate this on two settings where prior approaches required per-task engineering. For agile locomotion, a single policy acquires multiple long-horizon skills that previously demanded per-task priors and separate training runs. For dexterous manipulation, we present the first fully-RL solutions to the nut-and-bolt and rod assembly tasks from the NIST board.
